Module 1: Getting Started with Python

1.1 Introduction to Python

Python Introduction

Welcome to the world of coding! 🚀
You are about to learn Python—one of the most popular, creative, and beginner-friendly programming languages on the planet.
Think of programming as giving superpowers to your computer. Just like you use English or Hindi to talk to your friends, you use Python to tell your computer, phone, or robot exactly what to do.
You do not need to write any code on this page. Just get ready for an exciting adventure!
When you're ready, click Next Lesson to discover what makes Python so special.
Features of Python
Why do millions of young creators choose Python? Here are four reasons:
Reads Like Plain English: Python code is clean and simple. You don't have to memorize strange, confusing symbols.
Super Versatile: You can use Python to build games, craft websites, analyze space data, or create smart AI bots.
Beginner-Friendly: Python gives friendly clues when you make a mistake, helping you fix your code quickly.
Works Everywhere: A Python program written on Windows runs smoothly on a Mac, Linux, or even a tiny mini-computer like a Raspberry Pi.
Click Next Lesson to see what real-world things you can build with Python!
Why Python?
Python isn't just for learning—it powers some of the coolest tools and games in the world!
Video Games: Game developers use Python to script mechanics and design characters.
Space Exploration: NASA and rocket scientists use Python to track satellites and study distant planets.
Entertainment: Platforms like YouTube, Netflix, and Spotify use Python to stream your favorite videos and suggest music.
Artificial Intelligence (AI): Python is the #1 language used to teach computers how to recognize faces, drive autonomous cars, and chat like real people.
If you can imagine it, you can build it with Python!
Click Next Lesson to see how a computer actually runs your code.
How Python programs execute
Have you ever wondered what happens after you click the Run button?
Computers do not speak human languages. They only understand 0s and 1s. That's where the Python Interpreter comes in!
You write the code in the code editor (e.g., in simple English words).
The Interpreter translates it: Python reads your instructions line by line, from top to bottom, like reading a comic book.
The Computer executes it: Your computer follows the instructions instantly and displays the result on your screen
Figure: Code Editor (print) ---> Python Interpreter (Translator) ---> Console Screen
Now that you know how it works behind the scenes, let's write your first command! Click Next Lesson.
The print() function
To make your computer speak or show a message on the screen, Python gives you a special command called the print() function.
Whatever you place inside the parentheses ( ) and quotation marks " " will be displayed in the output console.
All you need to do is click the Run Code button.
How It Works:
print: The name of the Python action (always in lowercase).
( ) Parentheses: The container that holds what you want to show.
" " Quotation Marks: Tell Python that this is literal text (called a string), so Python prints it exactly as typed, without the quotes.
Figure: Print Hey Welcome to Y Coders
Be Careful:
Python is case-sensitive!
print("Hey") is correct.
Print("Hey") with a capital P will cause a NameError because Python doesn't recognize it.
Click Next Lesson to learn how to leave secret notes in your code.
Comments (#) & Code Readability
As your programs grow, you'll want to add notes to remind yourself—or your teammates—what your code does. In Python, these notes are called comments.
To create a comment, start the line with the # symbol (hash / pound sign):
Output
Why Comments Matter:
Python completely ignores anything that comes after #. It will never appear on the output screen.
Comments make your code clean, readable, and easy to understand when you come back to it next week.

Chapter Review
Congratulations! 🏆
You've officially written and understood your first Python programs!
Figure: Course Flow
Here is a quick recap of the superpowers you unlocked in Chapter 1:
Python: A friendly, powerful coding language that reads like plain English.
Interpreter: Reads your code line by line from top to bottom and runs it.
print("message"): The command to display text on the screen. Always remember lowercase print, parentheses (), and quotation marks "".
Comments (#): Notes for humans that Python ignores. Use them to make your code neat and easy to understand.
Ready for Chapter 2? In the next chapter, we'll dive into Data Types & Variables and learn how computers remember game scores and player names!

1.2 Displaying Output

Output Intro

Welcome to your next coding level! 🎮

In programming, output is everything your computer displays back to you on the screen—like a high score, a game dialogue, or a mission alert.

So far, you’ve displayed simple greetings. In this chapter, you’ll unlock real console mastery: formatting messages cleanly, printing numbers alongside words, handling line breaks, and using Python’s superpower: f-strings!

No code needed on this page. Click Next Lesson to get started!

Printing Numbers & Text

Python treats plain words and pure numbers differently:

Text (Strings): Must always be wrapped in quotation marks " ".

Numbers: Can be printed directly without quotes!

Output

Why This Matters

When you put numbers in quotes like "100", Python sees them as plain letters (like a sticker). When you write 100 without quotes, Python recognizes it as a real number you can calculate with!

Click Next Lesson to discover how to write longer stories across multiple lines.

Multiline Strings

What if you want to print a long poem, a character speech, or ASCII banner art without writing print() ten times?

Python gives you a special trick: Triple Quotes (""" or ''').

Output

Anything inside """ keeps its exact layout—including every enter, blank line, and space!

Click Next Lesson to test this out with a quiz.

Quiz: Multiline Strings

Which symbol allows you to write a single string that spans across multiple lines?

Tap an option below to answer:

A: """ (Triple quotes)

Correct Answer! 🎉
Wrapping text between triple quotes """ or ''' lets you write across multiple lines freely.

B: // (Double forward slash)

Incorrect, give it another shot!
In Python, // is an arithmetic division operator, not a text symbol.

C: ### (Triple hash)

Incorrect, give it another shot!
A hash symbol # creates comments, which Python ignores completely.

D: (( )) (Double parentheses)

Incorrect, give it another shot!
Parentheses group instructions; they do not create multiline text.

Print Multiple Values

You don’t have to create separate print() lines for every item. You can display multiple values inside a single print() by separating them with a comma ,.

Print Newline (\n)

Want your output to drop down to the next line without writing multiple print() commands? Use the magic escape code: \n (newline).

Think of \n like pressing the Enter key on your keyboard right in the middle of your sentence!

Output

\n doesn't insert a space; it pushes the next word to a brand-new line.

B: Red\nBlue\nGreen

Incorrect, give it another shot!
Python treats \n as an action command, not ordinary text letters.

C: Three lines with Red, then Blue, then Green

Correct Answer! 🎉
Each \n acts like pressing Enter, splitting the three colors onto their own lines.

D: An error occurs.

Incorrect, give it another shot!
\n is a completely valid escape sequence in Python.

Common Errors When Printing

Every coder runs into bugs—here are 3 common ones to watch out for:

1. Forgetting the Comma:

Fix: Put a comma , between different values: print("Coins:", 50).

2. Mixing Up Slashes:

Fix: Always use backslash \n, not forward slash /n.

3. Mismatched Quotes:

Fix: Match double quotes with double quotes "..." or single with single '...'.

Python f-strings

While commas work fine, Python has a much cooler and cleaner way to mix variables and text: f-strings (formatted strings)!

To use an f-string:

Put the letter f right before the quotation mark.

Put any variable name inside curly braces { }.

Python automatically replaces {character} with "Pikachu" and {hp} with 120. It reads like a complete, natural sentence!

1.3 Comments

Introduction to Comments
Imagine you are doing a science experiment at school and writing notes in your lab notebook. You write down measurements, but you also write short notes to explain what those numbers mean.
In Python, you can do the exact same thing using comments.
Suppose you write this line to record the temperature of a greenhouse:
Output
If you forgot the # symbol and just typed:
Python would get confused and throw a SyntaxError because it tries to run your English notes as code!
Comments allow you to add helpful explanations directly inside your file without affecting how your program works.
Click Next Lesson to see how Python handles comments behind the scenes.
Understanding Python Comments
Whenever the Python interpreter sees the # symbol, it treats everything after it on that line as invisible. It simply skips right past it!
Let's look at a smart baking timer program:

What Happened Here?
Lines 1 and 4 start with #, so Python skips them completely.
In Line 3, Python executes print(25) and ignores # Minutes left to bake.
The comments help anyone reading the recipe code understand what it does, but they never clutter the output screen.
Click Next Lesson to learn the different ways to write comments!
Types of Comments
Coders use comments in three main ways depending on how much they want to explain:
1. Single-Line Comments
The entire line is dedicated to an explanation. It starts with #:
2. Inline Comments
A quick note placed at the end of an active line of code:
3. Multi-Line Notes
When you have a longer explanation, you can put a # at the start of each line:

1.4 Understanding Variables

Variable Introduction

So far, we have printed fixed numbers and words directly to the screen. But what if you need to remember information and use it later—like a player's score, the temperature of an incubator, or the name of a space probe?

This is where variables come in!

Think of a variable as a labeled storage box. You put a sticky label on the outside (the variable's name) and place an item inside (the value). Whenever your program needs that item, it just looks up the box by its label!

Figure: A labeled box with the label "player_name" holding the card "Leo"

Click Next Lesson to see how to create your first variable box!

Create Variables

Creating a variable in Python is called assignment. You write the variable name, use the equals sign =, and then give it a value:

How It Works:

planet: The name of your variable (the label on the box).

=: The assignment operator. It tells Python: "Take the value on the right and store it inside the box on the left."

"Mars": The data being stored.

Python stores this information in memory instantly.

Click Next Lesson for a quick check!

Quiz: Spot the Variable

In the following line of code, what is the variable name?

Tap an option below to answer:

A: 120
Incorrect, give it another shot! 120 is the numerical value stored inside the variable, not the variable's name.

B: speed

speed is the label used to identify and store the value in memory.

C: =
Incorrect, give it another shot! The = symbol is the assignment operator used to put the value into the variable.

D: "speed"
Incorrect, give it another shot! Variable names are never written inside quotation marks.

Printing Variables

To see what is stored inside a variable box, pass its name directly to the print() function without quotation marks:

print("dino_name") with quotes prints the literal word dino_name.

A: Falcon on both lines

B: animal followed by Falcon

Correct Answer! 🎉
"animal" prints as plain text, while animal retrieves the stored value "Falcon".

C: animal on both lines

Incorrect, give it another shot! The second statement accesses the variable, which holds "Falcon".

D: A NameError occurs.

Incorrect, give it another shot! Both statements are completely valid Python.

A: Variable names cannot store text.
Incorrect, give it another shot! Variables can hold text, numbers, and many other data types.

Python executes line by line. When line 1 runs, captain has not been created yet, raising a NameError.

C: The word print must be capitalized.

A Common Error: Assigning Undefined Variables

In Python, the variable on the right side of = must already exist! You cannot copy data from an empty, non-existent box into another box.

Rule to Remember:

Left side of =: The box you are filling.

Right side of =: The value or existing box you are taking from.

Change Variables

Why are they called variables? Because their values can vary (change) over time!

When you put a new value into an existing variable, the old value is replaced:

1.5 Data Type
Introduction to Data Types
In real life, different items serve different purposes. You can wear a jacket, but you can't drink it. You can drink a glass of water, but you can't wear it!
Computers work the exact same way. When you give information to Python, it needs to know what kind of data it is so it knows what it is allowed to do with it.
For example:
You can do math with numbers (like 10 + 5 = 15).
But you can’t subtract a pet's name from a shoe size!
In Python, the category or form of data you give to a variable is called its Data Type.
Click Next Lesson to discover the four most important data types every coder uses!

1.8 Type Conversion

Intro to Type Conversion

In coding, data doesn't always arrive in the exact form you need.

A user types the number 25, but Python hands it to you as the text string "25".

A stopwatch measures a race time of 14.8 seconds, but your leaderboard only awards whole-second points.

When you transform data from one data type into another, it is called Type Conversion (or data type transformation).

It's like melting ice into liquid water: the core information is still there, but its state has changed so you can use it in a brand-new way!

Click Next Lesson to learn the two ways Python converts data.

Type Casting vs Type Coercion

There are two distinct ways data types change in Python:

Type Coercion (Implicit / Automatic):

Python does the work for you automatically behind the scenes.

You don’t write any special conversion commands.

Example: When you add an integer and a float, Python quietly upgrades the integer to a float so no decimal precision is lost.

Type Casting (Explicit / Manual):

You specifically command Python to change the data type using conversion functions like int(), float(), or str().

Example: Converting text input into a number using int("50").

Click Next Lesson to see automatic conversion in action!

Here is your master recap for controlling program flow:

else: Runs when the if condition is False.

3.4 Loop Controls (break and continue)

Introduction

Usually, a loop runs until its condition becomes False or until it reaches the end of a list.

But in real-world programs, unexpected things happen:

What if a game character loses all lives? You want to stop the game loop immediately, without waiting for the timer to run out!

What if an inspection robot spots a cracked egg on a conveyor belt? You want to skip packing that one egg and jump straight to the next one!

To take precise control of your loops, Python provides two special steering wheels:

break: The Emergency Brake (stops and exits the loop immediately).

continue: The Skip Button (skips the rest of the current turn and jumps to the next turn).

Click Next Lesson to learn about break!

The break Statement

The break statement immediately stops a loop in its tracks. As soon as Python hits break, it abandons the loop completely and jumps down to the code outside the loop!

Even though range(1, 10) was ready to count all the way to 9, as soon as number reached 4, break ran, and the loop stopped instantly!

What happens when you put a loop inside another loop? You get a Nested Loop!

Sports Practice: Your coach tells you to do 3 sets (outer loop) of 5 jumping jacks (inner loop).

The Outer Loop controls how many big rounds you do.
The Inner Loop runs completely from start to finish on every single turn of the outer loop!

Module 4: Storing & Organizing Collections
4.1 Strings in Depth

Collections

Welcome to Module 4! 🎒

Until now, each of our variables held just a single piece of data (like score = 100 or speed = 45.5).

In this module, you will learn about Collections. A collection is a container that lets you store and organize multiple pieces of data together under one name!

You actually already know the most famous collection in Python: the String! A string is an ordered collection of characters (letters, numbers, spaces, and emojis) all linked together like cars on a train.

Click Next Lesson to inspect strings under a microscope!

Python Strings

In Python, a string is an ordered sequence of characters wrapped in quotation marks.

Every single letter, number, punctuation mark, and space has its own specific spot in line:

Output

The len() function counts every single character in the collection—including blank spaces!

Creating Strings

Python gives you three ways to create strings:

Double Quotes (" "): phrase = "Space Station"

Single Quotes (' '): phrase = 'Space Station'

Triple Quotes (""" """ or ''' '''): Perfect for multiline dialogues, poems, or ASCII art!

Output

Concatenate Strings (Join)

To glue two or more strings together into one long sentence, use the + operator:

Output

(Remember: Python does not add a space automatically with +. You must add " " yourself if you want a space between words!)

Escape Sequences

What happens if you want quotation marks inside your text sentence?

If you type print("He said "Hello!" to me"), Python gets confused by the extra quotes. To fix this, use an escape sequence with a backslash \:

\": Prints a literal double quote without confusing Python.

\': Prints a literal single quote / apostrophe.

\n: Pushes the following text to a brand-new line.

\t: Inserts a tab (4 spaces).

Access Characters of a String

Because a string is an ordered collection, every character has an address number called an index:

Plaintext

String:   P  Y  T  H  O  N

Index:    0  1  2  3  4  5

Neg:     -6 -5 -4 -3 -2 -1

Zero-Based Indexing: The first character is always at index [0].

Negative Indexing: Index [-1] gives the very last character, [-2] gives the second-last, and so on!

Watch Out For IndexError:

blocks.content: 4.4 Python Sets
Python Sets
Imagine you collect superhero stickers. If your friend gives you a sticker you already have, you don’t need two identical stickers in your album—you only care about having one unique copy of each!
In Python, this is exactly what a Set does!
A Set is a special collection with two superpowers:
No Duplicates Allowed: A set automatically throws away any duplicate items. Every item inside is guaranteed to be 100% unique!
Unordered: Items don’t sit in numbered index slots like lists or tuples. They float inside the collection like marbles in a bag.
Click Next Lesson to create your first set!
Creating Sets
You create a set by placing items inside curly braces { } separated by commas:
Output
Notice that the repeated 2s and 3s were instantly erased! Also, the order might look scrambled on your screen because sets are unordered.
The Empty Set Trap:
Writing {} creates an empty Dictionary, not a set! To create an empty set, you must use the set() function:
empty_chest = set() # The correct way to make an empty set!

| C: 2 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! There are three different gem names in the collection. |

| D: A TypeError occurs. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Writing duplicate values in a set is valid—Python just cleans them up for you. |
Add and Update Sets
Because sets do not have index slots like [0], you cannot use indexing to change items. Instead, Python gives us two methods:
.add(item): Adds a single new item.
.update(collection): Adds multiple items at once from a list or another set!

Python Dictionaries
In lists and tuples, you look up items using index numbers like 0, 1, or 2.
But what if you want to look up an item by its name instead of a number?
In a real dictionary, you look up a Word to find its Definition.
In a contact list, you look up a Friend's Name to find their Phone Number.
In a video game, you look up a Stat Name (like "Speed") to find its Value (like 85).
For this, Python gives us one of its most powerful collections: the Dictionary!
A dictionary stores information in Key-Value Pairs:
Key: The unique label you search for (e.g., "Health").
Value: The data attached to that label (e.g., 100).
Click Next Lesson to create your first dictionary!
Create Dictionaries
You create a dictionary by placing key: value pairs inside curly braces { }, separated by commas:

4.6 Data Structure Conversions
Python Conversion
You’ve now met the four main collection types in Python:
Lists ([ ]): Changeable and ordered.
Tuples (( )): Locked and unchangeable.
Sets ({ }): Unordered and duplicate-free.
Dictionaries ({k: v}): Labeled key-value lookups.
Sometimes you start with one collection type, but need to shape-shift it into another:

In Python, that shortcut button is called a Function.

5.3 Variable Scope (Local vs Global)
Global Variable
In programming, Scope refers to where in your code a variable can be seen and used.
Think of a Global Variable like a giant public clock in the middle of a town square:
Anyone walking through the town can look up and see what time it is.
Any house or shop in the town can use that time.
A variable created in your main code outside of any function is called a Global Variable. It belongs to the whole program, and any function can read its value!
Click Next Lesson to see a global variable in action!

| Incorrect, give it another shot! planet is accessible across the entire file. |
Local Variable
Now, what about variables created inside a function?
Think of a Local Variable like a secret notebook locked inside your personal bedroom desk drawer:
You can read and write in it while you are in your room.
But nobody outside on the street can see it!
Any variable created inside a function's indented body is called a Local Variable. It is born when the function starts running, and it is completely destroyed the moment the function finishes!
Click Next Lesson to see what happens when you try to peek inside!

Why Did It Crash?
Because secret_code was local to secret_mission(). The moment the function ended, secret_code vanished from memory! The outside world has no idea it ever existed.
Why Is Local Scope Important?
You might wonder: "Why doesn't Python just make every variable global?"
Here are the 3 big reasons why local variables are a lifesaver:
No Name Clashes: If you name a variable total inside one function, and another programmer names a variable total inside a different function, they will never clash or overwrite each other!
Self-Contained Code: Functions are independent little machines. You can copy a function into another game without worrying about breaking existing variables.
Memory Cleanup: Once a function finishes its work, Python wipes its local variables clean to free up memory on your device!

| D: 0 |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Python will not invent a default value for an out-of-scope variable. |

| Incorrect, give it another shot! Python allows different functions to use the exact same variable names without any error. |

blocks.content: 6.1 Using Modules
Introduction

Imagine a carpenter building a dining table. When they need to smooth a wooden board, they don't invent sandpaper or build an electric saw from raw steel—they simply reach into their toolbox and pick the ready-made tool!
In Python, that pre-built toolbox is called a Module.

A Module is a file packed with ready-to-use functions written by other experienced developers. Instead of writing long, difficult formulas for daily tasks—like calculating compound interest, measuring construction areas, or generating random invoice numbers—you simply import the module and use its tools right away!
Python comes with built-in modules for everyday livelihood tasks:
math: For carpentry, construction, and money calculations.
random: For lucky draws, raffle contests, and team selectors.
csv: For reading grocery store inventories and school spreadsheets.
Click Next Lesson to open your first digital toolbox!
Importing Modules
To use a module in your program, write the import keyword at the very top of your code.
Let’s import Python's built-in math module to solve two common real-life problems:
Once imported, we use dot notation (module_name.function()) to call its tools:

math.ceil(number): Rounds a decimal UP to the nearest whole integer.
Real life: If a fruit juice recipe needs 3.2 oranges, you cannot buy 0.2 of an orange at the fruit market—you must buy 4 full oranges!

math.sqrt(number): Finds the square root.
Real life: If a square room has an area of 64 square meters, how long is one wall?

| D: cartons = math->sqrt(144) |

Renaming Modules (import ... as)
In daily business or store accounting, you might have to call math functions dozens of times. Typing math. over and over can slow you down.

Now, instead of typing math.ceil(), you simply type m.ceil()!

Introduction
As you build practical programs for daily life, you don't always need big new tools. Sometimes, knowing a few small "handy tricks" makes your code shorter, cleaner, and bug-free!
In this lesson, we will explore four essential everyday Python concepts:
Assignment Operators: Quick shortcuts for adding up grocery bills and pocket money.
Truthy & Falsy Values: How Python automatically checks whether a shopping bag or bank balance is empty.
The None Keyword: How computers represent an empty shelf or an unassigned receipt.
The pass Statement: The "under-construction" sign that keeps your code from crashing while you plan new features.
Click Next Lesson to learn your first math shortcut!
Assignment Operators
In a local grocery shop, when a customer adds a pack of biscuits to their cart, the cashier doesn't rewrite the entire receipt—they simply add to the existing total.
Instead of writing bill = bill + 20, Python gives you assignment shortcuts:
These shortcuts save typing, reduce mistakes, and make your code look professional!

Truthy & Falsy
In Python, every single piece of data can be tested in an if condition, even if it is not explicitly True or False.
Think of it like checking a customer's shopping cart:
If the cart is completely empty, it acts like False.
If the cart has even one item, it acts like True!
Python calls these Truthy and Falsy values:
The Falsy Values (Things that act like False):
0 and 0.0 (zero balance)
"" (empty text string)
[] (empty shopping list)
{} (empty inventory dictionary)
None (empty / no value)
False
The Truthy Values:
Everything else! Any number other than zero (like 5 or -12), and any non-empty text (like "Apples").
Click Next Lesson to see why this is super helpful in daily life!
Example: Checking an Empty Shopping Basket
Because empty collections are falsy, you can check if a customer has items in their cart in a single, natural line:
Output
The Common Truthy Trap to Avoid:
Look at this common beginner mistake when comparing prices:
A beginner thinks this checks if both fruits cost more than 50. But Python actually checks:
Is apple_price > 50?
AND is orange_price truthy (non-zero)?
Because orange_price is a number like 40, it is always truthy! To do real price comparisons, always write out both sides clearly: if apple_price > 50 and orange_price > 50:.
Quiz: Evaluating Truthy & Falsy
A bakery manager wrote this code to check inventory:
What will appear on the bakery display?
Tap an option below to answer:

| A: Fresh bread available today! |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! bread_loaves is 0. In Python, the number 0 is a falsy value! |

| B: Sold out! Baking fresh batch tomorrow. |
| Correct Answer! 🎉 Because 0 evaluates to False, the if block is skipped and the else block executes! |

| C: Both messages |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Only one branch of an if-else statement can run. |

| D: A TypeError occurs. |
| Incorrect, give it another shot! Testing numbers directly in an if condition is completely legal Python. |
The None Keyword
What if a store shelf has no product placed on it yet, or a customer hasn't selected a home delivery address?
In Python, we represent the complete absence of a value with the keyword None.
None does not mean zero 0, and it does not mean an empty string ""—it literally means "Nothing exists here":
Output
Also, if you write a function that performs an action (like printing a receipt) without an explicit return statement, Python automatically returns None!
The pass Statement
Imagine a carpenter building a house: they build the walls first, but they leave an open doorway space where the wooden door will be installed next week.
In Python, if you write an if statement, loop, or function, Python does not allow you to leave its body empty. Even leaving a comment causes an IndentationError!
To leave a clean "under-construction" placeholder without crashing your program, use the pass keyword:

The pass statement does nothing when executed, but it keeps Python happy and prevents your program from crashing while you plan your next steps!
